examples: I can't complain in front of my children.
Since I promised, I can't very well refuse.
With the teacher right there, I can't fiddle with my phone.
Having spoken so forcefully in front of everyone, I can't back down now.
With my parents watching, it's hard to wear flashy clothes.
Since I once said I would do it, I'll take responsibility to the end.
fields.explain:
Gives the reason why it is “hard to do X” because of a barrier of face or social pressure; often used with ～わけにはいかない／にくい／しかない／ざるを得ない.
The tone is inward and self-imposed; usually used in the first person or about someone close.
Neutral to slightly formal; can be used in both spoken and written language.

• Meaning: because you are in front of someone / to save face / because you have already said or done something, it is hard to do the opposite, so you must keep up appearances or keep your word.
• Nuance: self-imposed restraint, social pressure or concern for face; usually tied to the speaker or someone on the speaker's side.
• N + の手前 emphasizes “in front of …, so it is awkward”; V + 手前 emphasizes “having already …, I cannot take it back”.
fields.notes:
• Derives from the original meaning “the front / the near side”; from there it developed the meaning “in front of others → saving face”.
• Often combined with structures of impossibility: ～わけにはいかない／にくい／づらい／しかない／ざるを得ない to emphasize the obligation.
• Can be used indirectly to decline or explain politely: “上司の手前、今回は見送ります”.
mistakes: Confusing the spatial meaning of “手前” with the grammar point meaning “face” → wrong context.
The second clause does not express a constraint (e.g. a sentence describing a scene) → unnatural.
Using it to carelessly justify negative behavior → sounds like an excuse and is not polite.

examples: The old days may have been different, but now information spreads instantly on social media.
A child might get away with it, but an adult can't use an excuse like that.
Whatever the truth of the inside story, we shouldn't be swayed by rumors.
Japanese pronunciation is another matter, but the grammar is systematic.
An expert would be one thing, but a layperson shouldn't make judgments on their own.
fields.explain:
Used to “set aside” one item from the scope of discussion in order to emphasize the main argument.
Part A is usually something remote from the speaker (他人、昔、子ども…), emphasizing “I can't say for sure”.
Part B is usually a standard, a rule, the current situation, a criticism or a suggestion.
The tone is formal; in casual conversation it can be replaced with “〜はともかく”.

• Presents an exception, “unknown / not discussed”, about A in order to emphasize a firm judgment about B.
• “ならいざ知らず”: grants that A might be acceptable (a supposition) in order to deny B more strongly.
• Nuance: polite, a little old-fashioned; strongly associated with written language, speeches and commentaries.
• The second clause often comes with structures of evaluation/difficulty/unacceptability.
fields.notes:
• “いざ” originally means “at the crucial moment”; in this pattern it creates the nuance “hard to say for sure”.
• With a complex clause: 結果がどうなるかはいざ知らず、準備だけは万全に。 (acceptable, but written language)
• Not used for direct questions; this pattern affirms the argument in the second clause.
mistakes: Attaching it directly to a verb without nominalizing it: incorrect. You need の/こと: 彼が来るのはいざ知らず…
The second clause should not be purely objective information; it should be an evaluation or a rule.
Confusing it with ともかく: いざ知らず has the nuance “unknown, can't say for sure” and is more formal.

rows: Nuance of “can't say for sure”; formal
<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>はさておき…
Reverses expectations; no sense of “don't know”

examples: I can't read even hiragana, let alone kanji.
I never even left the prefecture, let alone traveled abroad.
Day after day, I couldn't even take a lunch break, let alone a day off.
Forget manners — can't you even say hello?
He can speak not only Japanese but even English.
fields.explain:
Used to “lower” the point of comparison in order to highlight how serious or surprising the situation is.
Suitable for written language, commentary and complaints; carries a strong nuance of criticism when used with negatives.
In conversation, さえ is more natural than すら; but with はおろか, both すら and さえ are acceptable.

• Emphasizes the degree of surprise: not only N1, but even N2 (a lower level) is not/hardly/…
• Order: N1 is the larger or obvious scope; N2 is the smallest, minimal example.
• “すら” has a more formal nuance than “さえ”; both emphasize the extreme case.
• Usually used with negatives: ない／できない／むずかしい…, but can also be affirmative in some contexts.
fields.notes:
• For a softer tone, use “〜はもちろん/〜はもとより”; for a stronger one, keep “はおろか”.
• N2 should be the smallest example, clearly “minimal”, so the sentence is logical and sharp.
• When emphasizing something positive, choose carefully to avoid sounding sarcastic.
mistakes: Reversing the order of degree: making N2 bigger than N1 makes the sentence illogical. Make N2 the minimum.
Putting a verb directly after はおろか without nominalizing it → incorrect: “食べるはおろか” → correct: “食べることはおろか”.
Confusing it with はもちろん: はおろか usually goes with negative statements and has stronger emphasis.

rows: N はおろか、N2 すら/さえ…
<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>はおろか<ruby>氷<rt>こおり</rt></ruby>すらない
<ruby>上達<rt>じょうたつ</rt></ruby>どころか<ruby>悪化<rt>あっか</rt></ruby>した
N1 of course, and also N2
<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>はもちろん<ruby>中国<rt>ちゅうごく</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>も
Uses a small criterion to evaluate the whole
<ruby>服装<rt>ふくそう</rt></ruby>からしてだらしない

examples: Not just business management — even replying to emails is behind.
He taught himself not only Japanese but even English.
You forgot your own phone number, never mind your address?
Because of the rain, not only the match but even the ceremony was canceled.
She handled not only preparing the documents but even the meeting preparations all by herself.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to highlight that the scope extends to something unexpected (N2).
More neutral in formality than “すら”; suits a wide range of contexts.
N2 should still be a “minimal/peripheral” example to keep the logic of the emphasis.

• Similar to “はおろか〜すら/さえ”, but “まで” highlights the extended scope: “even … too”.
• Less old-fashioned in nuance than “すら”; natural in conversation and writing.
• The second clause can be affirmative (it happens even to N2) or negative (not even N2).
fields.notes:
• “まで” is flexible: it can be used with verbs, quantities and time ranges to broaden the statement.
• To emphasize the “surprising minimum”, “すら/さえ” is more effective. To emphasize all-encompassing scope, choose “まで”.
mistakes: Making N2 bigger than N1 breaks the logic of the emphasis. Make N2 lower/more peripheral than N1.
Dropping は after N1: an easy mistake in writing. The standard structure is: N1はおろか、N2まで…
Confusing it with はもちろん: はおろか is strong and usually implies something unexpected; はもちろん is neutral/affirmative listing.

<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>はおろか<ruby>氷<rt>こおり</rt></ruby>までない
N はおろか、N2 すら/さえ…
“すら” is more formal/old-fashioned; “さえ” is colloquial
<ruby>基礎<rt>きそ</rt></ruby>はおろか<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>すらできない
Not only N1 but also N2
<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>はもちろん<ruby>中国語<rt>ちゅうごくご</rt></ruby>まで<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す
No “まで/すら”; strong negative nuance
<ruby>改善<rt>かいぜん</rt></ruby>どころか<ruby>悪化<rt>あっか</rt></ruby>した

examples: He can't even give an ordinary greeting, let alone use keigo.
I've been so busy that I haven't even eaten out, let alone traveled.
I can't believe they can't even read hiragana, let alone kanji.
We're short not only on budget but even on staff.
She can speak not only English but even French.
For your health, you should start by reconsidering the fact that you're not even getting enough sleep, let alone exercise.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize that N2 “goes beyond the expected level”; N1 serves as the stronger standard of comparison.
Often carries a nuance of criticism or negative evaluation; it can be used in affirmative sentences, but then sounds showy or literary.
N1 is mostly a noun. With verbs/adjectives, nominalize with の/こと to sound natural.
Not used in very casual everyday situations; suited to written language, presentations and essays.

• Core meaning: “N1 goes without saying; even N2…”, expressing that N2 is beyond expectations; N1 is the higher or more obvious level.
• Often used with a negative clause to emphasize a lack or impossibility: ～も/すらできない, ～すらない.
• Order of degree: N1 (stronger/harder/more important) ＞ N2 (weaker/more basic). If N2 isn't achieved, N1 is “out of the question”.
• Slightly stiff nuance, leaning toward written language/speeches; can carry criticism or exaggeration.
• Variants with まで/すら make “even/to the extent of” stronger than も.
fields.notes:
• Choose an N1 that is “stronger” than N2 in difficulty/importance: 漢字(難) ＞ ひらがな(易).
• In affirmative sentences, まで/すら are more natural than も and add emphasis.
• Avoid overusing it in casual speech; in conversation use ～はもちろん, ～だって/～すら instead.
mistakes: Reversing the degree: choosing an N1 weaker than N2 → breaks the logic of the emphasis.
Using it carelessly in affirmative sentences → the nuance is off; in affirmative sentences, prefer まで/すら.
Attaching it directly to a verb without nominalizing → unnatural: × 食べるはおろか → ◯ 食べることはおろか.
Confusing it with ～どころか: ～はおろか means “going further in the same direction”, not “the opposite”.

rows: N1 is stronger than N2; emphatic nuance, slightly stiff
<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>はおろか、ひらがなも<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>めない
Contrastive comparison; does not require an N1/N2 pair on the same scale
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>むどころか、<ruby>徹夜<rt>てつや</rt></ruby>した
More neutral; not necessarily strongly emotional
<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>はもちろん、フランス<ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>も<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>せる
No N1 needed; focuses emphasis on the item marked with すら/さえ
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>ですら<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っている

examples: Once you start listing the flaws, there's no end to it.
If you start worrying, there's no end to it, so let's focus on what we can do now.
I could give endless examples, but I'll mention only the typical ones.
If you start wanting more, there'll be no end to it.
There's no end to the complaints we could list, so let's stop here.
fields.explain:
Often used with verbs meaning “to start bringing up”: 言い出す,挙げる,数え上げる,心配する,文句を言う.
Used in discussions to cut a long list short and bring the conversation back to the main point.
In spoken language ～たら／～ときりがない can be used, but in standard JLPT usage ～ばきりがない is common.

• “If … there is no end/no limit”; once you start doing/listing/demanding, it goes on forever.
• Often used for complaints, examples, desires, worries… that could go on endlessly.
• Nuance of warning and restraint: implies “don't go down that path any further”.
fields.notes:
• “きり/切り” originally means “limit, stopping point”. “きりがない” = “there is no stopping point”.
• Often placed before a concluding clause to cut a list short: ～ばきりがないが、要点だけ述べる。
• “欲を言えば/言い出せば” has a self-reflective nuance, advising restraint.
mistakes: Confusing it with “限りがない”: that one describes the property of being “unlimited”, not the conditional structure “if…, it's endless”.
Missing “ば/たら/と”: ×言い出すきりがない → correct: 言い出せばきりがない.
Using it for a one-time action that ends immediately → not suitable (this pattern implies going on endlessly).
The JLPT often tests fixed phrases: 欠点を言い出せばきりがない／例を挙げればきりがない.

rows: If you do it, it's endless
<ruby>例<rt>れい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>挙<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げればきりがない
<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>したら/ときりがない
Adjective / describes a state, unlike the conditional “if…, then”
<ruby>宇宙<rt>うちゅう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>りがない
Used on its own as a comment

examples: If you had just asked me, I could have helped you.
If I had gone to the hospital sooner, it would have healed.
Keeping quiet would have been fine, but saying something unnecessary caused a problem.
An apology to him would have settled it, but being stubborn made the relationship worse.
If it hadn't rained, we could have gone out.
fields.explain:
Usually used when the speaker feels regret or dissatisfaction about the current result.
Can carry a hint of gentle reproach toward the other person: “if only…”, “you should have…”.
Not used in cheerful, everyday contexts.
Often goes with emotional expressions: のに, くせに, ったら, but with a stronger nuance.

～ば～ものを expresses regret, dissatisfaction or reproach: “if only…, then it would have…, and yet…”. The speaker thinks that if the condition in the first clause had happened, the result would have been better, but in reality it did not.

•
Nuance: regret + mild reproach, or dissatisfaction.

•
Context: written language, serious conversation, emotional.

•
Logical structure:

(If A had happened) → (B would have been better), but in reality it wasn't.

•
Logical example:
If you had spoken up sooner, we could have avoided this… (but you didn't).
fields.notes:
• This pattern has the feel of “if only… it would have…”, but also implies “and yet it wasn't done”.
• Often appears in written language, stories, films, or emotionally charged dialogue.
• Not used for simple advice, because the emotional nuance is quite strong.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～のに in JLPT questions – note that if the sentence contains regret or reproach, choose ～ば～ものを.
Forgetting to conjugate the verb into the ba-form (conditional) before using ものを.
Not used in cheerful or very polite conversation – it easily sounds unnatural.
ものを is usually not followed by a command or request.

rows: <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えばよかった のに。
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>え ばよかった。

examples: Old, worn books are lined up on the shelf.
His clothes look a bit countrified, but they suit his personality.
My daughter speaks in a grown-up way for her age.
The old-fashioned turns of phrase are what make this novel appealing.
This street has a slightly shabby, run-down atmosphere.
fields.explain:
Mostly used to modify nouns:古びた町並み／大人びた顔立ち／田舎びた店。
To describe a current state: ～びている (このホテルは古びている)。
Written-language nuance, evocative; often used in literature, criticism and description.
Expresses a subjective evaluation based on outward impressions.

• Expresses “having the look of / a touch of / a hint of …”, focusing on outward impressions or flavor.
• The nuance can be positive (大人びた = mature), neutral (昔びた = with an old-time feel) or negative (田舎びた = countrified, 古びた = worn and old).
• Usually used as a noun modifier. As a predicate, use “～びている”.
• Limited productivity: only certain combinations are natural; it cannot be attached to just any noun.
fields.notes:
• Many combinations are set or customary: 古びた／田舎びた／大人びた／昔びた／場末びた／芝居びた。
• “～びた” is a past-form noun modifier but does not indicate past time; it is just a modifying form. To express past tense, use “～びていた”。
• With neutral/positive words: 大人びた (praise); with words of negative evaluation: 田舎びた (slightly disparaging).
mistakes: Misunderstanding “～びた” as past tense: it is not. It is the modifying form of ～びる.
Attaching “～びた” to any noun: many combinations are unnatural (×ITびたパソコン).
Using bare “～びた” as a predicate: use “～びている/～びていた” at the end of a sentence.
Confusing it with ～っぽい: ～っぽい is colloquial and broader in meaning; they are not interchangeable in every case.

rows: A look/air of “having the feel of …”
Usually modifies N; derived from ～びる
<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>びた<ruby>雰囲気<rt>ふんいき</rt></ruby>
Colloquial, broad scope, sometimes means “prone to …”
Literary; often used in the form ～めいた
<ruby>皮肉<rt>ひにく</rt></ruby>めいた<ruby>言<rt>いいかた</rt></ruby>い<ruby>方<rt></rt></ruby>
<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>ぶった<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>

examples: My daughter has suddenly become very grown-up.
Over the years, this chair has become old and worn.
Even though they've lived in the city for a long time, there's still something countrified about them.
That text looks deliberately old-fashioned.
For his age, he speaks in a calm, mature way.
fields.explain:
Describes a change in, or a characteristic of, appearance or atmosphere: ～びてくる／～びている.
Written/descriptive in nature; in spoken language it is often replaced with ～っぽくなる in some contexts.
Nuance of “looks like / seems”, without the strong sense of “pretending” that ～ぶる has.

• Expresses “becoming like / taking on a quality of …” in appearance, flavor or feel.
• Usually an intransitive verb, with no direct object.
• Evaluative value: can be positive (大人びる = mature), or slightly negative (田舎びる = countrified; 古びる = to become old and worn).
• Not every noun combines naturally with ～びる; most are customary combinations.
fields.notes:
• Some bases come from i-adjectives: 古い→古びる; others are nouns: 大人→大人びる, 田舎→田舎びる.
• Usually written in kana; “びる” rarely has its own kanji.
• Not used with every noun: choose natural, customary combinations.
mistakes: Confusing “～びる” with “～ぶる”: ～ぶる means “to pretend / put on airs”, with a nuance of criticism; ～びる means “to have the look of / become”.
Using it with a direct object: it is mostly an intransitive verb and does not take を.
Making up unnatural combinations (×都会びる言い方 → use instead: 都会的な言い方/洗練された言い方).

rows: To become/take on the look of …
Stative verb / verb of change; neutral
Literary; often used in the form ～めいた

examples: That affectedly refined way of talking is grating.
fields.explain:
Often comes before:態度／口調／顔／発言。

“Acting/pretending to be …” when modifying a noun, with a sarcastic nuance.
fields.notes: Stress it with intonation to make it more sarcastic.
mistakes: Misunderstanding it as past tense.
